content:
Hi all, my background is mostly in Solidity development, not formal verification, Lean or compilers, so I'm sure some of my assumptions here are naive.

I'm not very satisfied with the options we currently have for verified EVM contracts. You can write Solidity and create a formal twin model of it (Certora, Verity, Tamaswap), which leaves you with another representation to keep in sync and a compiler you still have to trust. Or you can work much closer to Yul/EVM using existing Lean formalizations such as Nethermind's EVMYulLean or Powdr's EVM/Yul semantics, where higher-level protocol properties can get pretty painful to state and prove.

Trying to fix this, I started working on "LSC" (Lean Smart Contracts), a smart contracts "language" written directly in Lean 4 and compiled to EVM bytecode. I'm trying to extend the Yul formalization to support a higher level of abstraction. The contract itself is a Lean program, but it compiles down through the existing Yul/EVM work. The hope is to eventually prove properties at the source level and carry those proofs all the way down to the generated bytecode.

In the current v3, contracts are ordinary Lean functions in a Tx monad, so we can prove properties directly about the source program. lsc_reify then inspects the elaborated term, extracts the supported subset into a small AST, and generates a proof that the AST has the same meaning as the original function. (Lean code -> AST -> Yul -> EVM).

The Core to Yul compiler and its semantic preservation proofs are in LSC. For Yul to EVM I'm building on Powdr Labs' yul-compiler:

https://github.com/powdr-labs/yul-compiler

A few examples:

  • https://github.com/prevostc/lsc/blob/v3/Examples/Counter/Contract.lean
  • https://github.com/prevostc/lsc/blob/v3/Examples/Cpamm/Contract.lean

The reifier is here, although it's becoming a bit of a mess:

https://github.com/prevostc/lsc/blob/v3/Lsc/Lang/Reify.lean

It's still experimental. The accepted Lean fragment is small, the current external-call model doesn't cover reentrancy, and there are still gaps around constructors/deployment.

I'd be very interested in feedback from people working on Lean metaprogramming or compiler verification, especially on the reification/certificate approach and whether there's a cleaner way to structure it. But also more generally on whether this approach makes sense and is worth pursuing.

This is close to home: #Program verification > Blanc: EVM contracts proved on the exact deployed bytecode chases the same "properties of the bytes that deploy" goal from the other end. Blanc programs are already data at assembly altitude, so there is no reifier, and I pay for that in proof ergonomics. Notes from that side of the trade, read against v3 at 8421101:

Reifier. If I read certifyDenote right, the certificate is recovered after reification: reducible rfl, else a ~200-lemma simp only set in staged passes, then rfl, with firstDifferingBind to localise a miss. That would explain the heartbeat and "poison" comments and the per-index Atom.eval_var_n lemmas. The pattern that scales in Mathlib's reflective tactics (ring, omega, norm_num) is proof-producing reification: each step returns the Core node and a proof that its denotation equals exactly the subterm it consumed, composed through bind/ite congruence lemmas, with a local bind_assoc or unfold at the one point where you reassociate or inline a helper. The kernel then checks a proof shaped like the AST, the per-index lemmas disappear, and a failure names the step that broke (what firstDifferingBind reconstructs after the fact). Incrementally: a proof-producing monad normalisation first, then a syntactic reifier that is rfl-correct on the normal form. Neither changes the trust story.

End to end. Per your PROOF_CHAIN.md, no example is lifted to bytecode yet. Token through the call-free transport_* theorems looks like the cheapest one, with no realization premise. Vault and Cpamm need hCalls : CallsRealized (toCalls oracle); the only realised response I found upstream is the insufficient-balance failure, and powdr's README leaves success-and-return to the client. Is there a witness where a token call succeeds? It would be a symbolic run of the token's bytecode through powdr's relational Steps, one per callee. That cost is why I went total: Jaune's exec is total, so Blanc gets the callee's execution from a theorem rather than a premise (ForwardCall.lean), for arbitrary callee code, re-entry included. Two caveats: that directly buys properties true of any callee (FMINT's supply invariant against an arbitrary re-entering borrower, no lock); a vault that relies on its token behaving still needs a joint invariant with the token's real code, which in Blanc is a declared successor, not a result.

Vault offset. Your Shares has the same price shape as a Blanc étude, PRORATA. Stating the victim's loss per price quantum, v - p <= (B + 1) / (S + O) + 1 with (S, B) the pre-deposit supply and balance, stays small once supply exists and survives arbitrary coalition moves between the victim's deposit and exit, because the price never falls. And the attacker-side form (no coalition takes out more than it put in over any closed trace, donations included) needs at least two virtual shares: at one virtual share an exact-integer oracle found a five-step transcript that skims one wei. Your ⟨6⟩ is far from that edge and inflation_bound_raw holds at any offset; the boundary only bites for the no-profit form, and Offset admits decimals = 0.

Pins. #print axioms pins won't catch an agent weakening a statement. Checks already builds in CI, so example : <exact type> := thm beside each axiom pin makes proof refactors pass and statement changes fail loudly.

One question. IERC20.Spec takes success as a hypothesis, so nothing concludes that withdraw succeeds, and a vault whose withdraw always reverts satisfies vault_solvent and vault_no_unauthorized_extraction. Is a success-side token spec on the roadmap? For WETH10 that property is what pushed us to exact gas and deployment-rooted theorems; PRORATA doesn't claim it either. Overall: yes, worth pursuing, and I'd make one end-to-end instance the next milestone.

Disclaimer. I relied heavily on agents for drafting this reply, including reading and analyzing your codebase. My main human input was having already set up a project (and an agent work environment for it) that is highly adjacent to yours, which gives agents new PoVs in juxtaposition. Caveats re: hallucinations apply per usual; let me know if I am mischaracterizing any part of your project.

Well, thank you for you amazing feedback. I started working on it but in the meantime, I found out that verity is not what I initially thought it was. Verity is precisely what LSC is trying to achieve, but far ahead in terms of maturity and backed by the Ethereum Foundation. So I'll just archive LSC and use verity instead.
Thanks again :heart_hands:
